## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

Volume 2 is the practical companion to Volume 1. The Foreword describes it as "a set of practical methods and techniques for anticipating, preventing, and catching active human errors; and, more importantly, identifying and mitigating latent errors attributable to organizational factors" [V] (Foreword, p. i). It carries forward Volume 1's formula: "Reducing error and managing controls —by eliminating latent system weaknesses—is the human performance paradigm for achieving zero significant events" [V], written R + M → ØE with subscripts e and c [AP] (Foreword, p. i). The tools introduced in Volume 1, and others used to eliminate organisational weaknesses, are described here with good practices, supporting applications and cautions [AP] (Foreword, p. ii).

The handbook is explicit about what it is not. "This handbook is not a requirements document" [V]; the practices are "intended to be illustrative, not definitive" [V] (Foreword, pp. i–ii). Organisations are to assess their own needs and treat the volume as a menu: "No organization is expected to use every tool listed, but rather to see the handbook as a “menu” of tools used in various industries and select those appropriate for use in their organization" [V], and "Organizations should avoid changing their error prevention tools if the current tools and behavior standards presently in place are effective" [V] (Foreword, p. ii). The tools enhance, rather than replace, existing requirements such as the DOE Integrated Safety Management System, Quality Assurance and Conduct of Operations, and the DOE Guide to Good Practices series [AP] (Foreword, pp. i–ii).

Its central caution is that the tools are no substitute for competence and thought. "For the human performance tools to provide value in improving safety, workers first must possess a solid foundation in the technical fundamentals of the equipment, systems, and operational processes they work with" [V], and "Safety is not obtained by mindlessly applying human performance tools but rather by people conscientiously applying their knowledge, skills, experience and insights, as well as the tools to accomplish their work goals" [V] (Introduction, p. 1). The facility, its processes, its culture and its oversight all hold hidden flaws that can cause harm if work is done without thinking [AP] (Introduction, p. 1).

The volume divides the work three ways [AR] (Introduction, p. 1). Section 1 gives tools a single person can use on any task, whatever its hazard or complexity, without prompting or supervision. Section 2 gives tools that need two or more people, supervisory involvement and management support, chosen according to the work situation and its risks. Section 3 gives managers and supervisors methods for finding latent weaknesses in the organisation and the management system. The first two sections aim at active errors at the point of work; the third at the latent conditions that provoke error and weaken defences (Introduction, p. 1; Sec 3, p. 70).

## Part I: Framing and use (Foreword, Introduction)

### Audience and sources

The Foreword names three audiences [AP] (Foreword, p. i): workers who touch facility equipment and can change its status or configuration; scientists, engineers, procedure writers, trainers and other knowledge workers who create and modify "the paper plant" [V] and whose errors can enter the system and later cause events; and supervisors and managers looking for organisational weaknesses that raise the likelihood or consequences of error. A further aim is a common understanding of the standards and conditions for applying error detection and prevention methods, which the handbook calls "tools" [AP] (Foreword, p. i).

For the individual and work-team tools, the Foreword credits two INPO good-practice guides as the primary references, describing them as reflecting years of user experience among INPO's members and INPO's own evaluations, assistance visits, operating experience and benchmarking; DOE contractors' experience with several of the tools is offered as further evidence of their value [BT] (Foreword, p. i). The management tools draw on DOE and INPO publications and on books and articles about accident reduction [BT] (Foreword, p. i). The handbook was produced by DOE's Office of Health, Safety and Security (HSS), which invites comments [AP] (Foreword, p. ii).

### How each tool is presented

Every tool is set out under four headings [AP] (Introduction, pp. 1–2): an overview of purpose and limitations; cues for when to use it; recommended practices, described as the steps generally used in industry; and at-risk practices, the behaviours, beliefs, assumptions or conditions that undermine the tool. A footnote distinguishes the "at risk practices" label from formal risk analysis: at the activity level "risk" means the hazards of doing the work, while formal risk analysis leading to safety controls is the organisation's responsibility, and activity-level workers should concentrate on hazard awareness and the protection set in work controls [AP] (Introduction, p. 2, footnote *2). A second footnote treats "facility" as a generic word for the reader's own unit of work (projects for D&D, experiments for laboratory work) [AP] (Introduction, p. 1, footnote *1). The Introduction also points readers to the 2006 NNSA document on activity-level work planning and control for incorporating ISM and QA requirements [BT] (Introduction, p. 1).

### When to use which tool

A two-page matrix maps each Section 1 and Section 2 tool to work location (in the field, meaning operations, maintenance and field support; in the office, meaning engineering, science and technical support) and to work phase (before start or restart, performing, completing; problem solving; verification) [AP] (Introduction, pp. 3–4). The matrix is badly broken in conversion (see the integrity notes), so this reference does not reproduce its cell-by-cell assignments; each tool's own "Use This Tool" list is the reliable statement of when to apply it.

## Part II: Tools for individuals (Sec 1)

All of Part II is paraphrased from INPO-adapted material; see the header.

### Purpose and situational awareness

The individual tools exist to help a performer keep positive control of the work, meaning that what is intended to happen is what happens and nothing else [AP] (Sec 1, p. 5). Acting with that understanding takes time; the handbook argues that every human performance tool deliberately slows work down in order to speed it up overall, by avoiding the delays that follow events triggered by active errors, and that the tools give the performer time to think about what is happening, what will happen and what to do if things go differently [AR] (Sec 1, p. 5). The aim is to keep positive control at critical steps where error-free performance is essential for safety; the tools do not guarantee perfect performance but, used thoughtfully, greatly reduce the chance of error [AP] (Sec 1, p. 5).

Many of the individual tools are classed as situational-awareness tools, situational awareness being the accuracy of a person's current understanding of the task and conditions compared with actual conditions [AP] (Sec 1, p. 5). These tools are said to sharpen a person's ability to notice unsafe conditions and to be particularly helpful in skill-mode work; two of them, Procedure Use and Adherence and Validate Assumptions, are singled out as having particular value for rule-based work [AP] (Sec 1, p. 5).

### Task Preview

Before starting work the individual previews the task: reviewing procedures and documents for scope, sequence and critical steps, talking with people who have done the job before, and walking down the job site [AP] (Sec 1, p. 6). The preview is a structured, risk-based review from a human performance perspective: identify the critical steps, the errors possible at each and their likely consequences, the worst that could happen, the tools to apply, and the controls, contingencies and operating experience (in-house events, equipment history, personal and industry experience) [AP] (Sec 1, p. 6). It is used before a pre-job briefing, before starting a job, just before a critical step and after interruptions or long delays [AP] (Sec 1, p. 6). The practice is the S-A-F-E-R sequence: **S**ummarize the critical steps; **A**nticipate errors and error precursors for each; **F**oresee probable and worst-case consequences; **E**valuate controls and contingencies to prevent, catch and recover from errors; **R**eview previous experience and lessons learned [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 6–7). At-risk practices include skipping the document review, arriving unprepared, leaving out controls for each critical step, not voicing concerns and ignoring lessons from earlier work [AP] (Sec 1, p. 7).

### Job-Site Review

On arriving at the work location, the person spends a few minutes walking the area to build an accurate picture of indicators, equipment condition, environment, hazards and even fellow team members; doing so is said to establish a healthy sense of uneasiness and strengthen the questioning attitude [AP] (Sec 1, p. 8). The walk looks for industrial, radiological and environmental hazards; trip-sensitive equipment; the right system, equipment and component; critical parameters; error precursors at critical steps; and whether conditions match the procedure and briefing. The person then talks through unexpected hazards with co-workers or the supervisor, and removes hazards, installs defences or develops contingencies before proceeding [AP] (Sec 1, p. 8). Use cues include arrival on site, before touching risk-important equipment, during work-package walk-downs, when a hazard may be present and after long breaks [AP] (Sec 1, p. 8). At-risk practices include hurrying, treating repetitive work as routine and therefore risk-free, not discussing hazards and not voicing gut feelings [AP] (Sec 1, p. 9).

### Questioning Attitude — at the activity level

A questioning attitude makes people think about safety before acting and keeps their understanding of conditions accurate; it alerts them to hazards, warning signs, critical steps, error-likely situations and uncertainties, and prompts them to stop and resolve these before going on [AP] (Sec 1, p. 10). The handbook observes that people are generally reluctant to fear the worst, and that a questioning attitude counters the temptation to rationalise away a gut feeling that something is wrong; it favours facts over assumption and opinion, with questions such as *what if* and *why is this acceptable*, and facts depend on the reliability and accuracy of their source [AP] (Sec 1, p. 10). Without enough facts the performer should stop rather than risk a serious mistake [AP] (Sec 1, p. 10).

Cues for use include the Think step of self-checking; before an important step; when deciding; when uncertain, confused or doubtful; when there is a gut feeling; when conditions change unexpectedly; when plans, procedures and conditions conflict; after unexpected results or missing information; and on hearing what the handbook calls danger words, such as *I assume*, *probably*, *should be* or *we've always* [AP] (Sec 1, p. 10). The four-step practice is: stop, look and listen (pause periodically for a time-out, pause at a flag, name the doubt); ask questions (separate knowns from unknowns, consult independent and reliable sources, especially knowledgeable people, try "what if" or a devil's-advocate stance); proceed only if the uncertainty has been resolved with facts; otherwise stop, make the equipment and site safe, and notify the supervisor [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 10–11). At-risk practices include not taking time-outs, proceeding with open questions, believing nothing can go wrong, treating repetitive work as routine, bending reality to fit one's mental model, rationalising anomalies, accepting first impressions as fact, not understanding the basis of a procedure step, letting emotion rather than reason drive decisions, and accepting supporting evidence without questioning it [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 11–12).

### Questioning Attitude — work planning and preparation

The office version applies the same attitude to planning, judgment and decision-making on a product under development, making the person aware of uncertainty, assumptions, risk factors and the significance of a decision before proceeding [AP] (Sec 1, p. 13). A good pre-job briefing strengthens it by making hazards, critical steps, risk-important parameters and error-likely situations known in advance [AP] (Sec 1, p. 13). The handbook warns that "cookbooking" procedures, its term for mindless compliance, and over-reliance on rules of thumb encourage unthinking responses to problems that seem simple and eventually lead to rule-based errors; a questioning attitude helps prevent this [AR] (Sec 1, p. 13). Cues for use include relying on previously approved evaluations, designs or guidance for a current issue; unexpected results; decisions where a mistake would matter; the start of any critical activity however often it recurs; experiments, engineering evaluations, product reviews, calculations, drawing and design-criteria revisions and procurement reviews; uncertainty about compliance or about what success means; approving an engineering product; and root cause, apparent cause and troubleshooting work [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 13–14).

The practice is named F-A-C-T-S [AP] (Sec 1, p. 14). In the converted text the labelled steps are: Foresee technical activities that involve critical attributes, asking open-ended questions about inputs, methods, outputs, priorities and anything that does not seem right; Confirm knowns and unknowns for critical activities, verifying critical facts and their sources, finding inconsistencies and unverified assumptions, summarising critical parameters and recognising error precursors; and Test the current situation, anticipating consequences, inviting others' questions and a devil's advocate, asking a qualified person to verify the information, comparing against facility documentation and codes, and considering testing or alternate analysis; the list ends with stopping when unsure, not proceeding in the face of uncertainty and informing the supervisor [AP] (Sec 1, p. 14). (The step numbering after step 1 is lost in conversion; see the integrity notes.) At-risk practices include dismissing contrary views, making assumptions, using unsuitable rules of thumb, treating a source as infallible, cookbooking, rationalising anomalies, assuming the task is routine, ignoring weak signals, not asking for help, and not questioning adverse effects that could appear at later stages of a project or outside one's own scope [AP] (Sec 1, p. 15).

### Pause When Unsure

When confused or uncertain a person is in unfamiliar territory with no defined path, the knowledge-based performance mode, where the handbook puts the chance of error at 10 to 50 percent; so the best action when unsure is to stop and ask [AP] (Sec 1, p. 16). Everyone has the responsibility and authority to stop work while uncertainty persists, and some organisations use a graded "pause" or "time-out" [AP] (Sec 1, p. 16). DOE facilities have formal Stop Work processes for workers who believe conditions may be unsafe and for the organisation when work must be postponed for re-analysis; this tool supplements them, encouraging deliberate and mindful work and treating a pause as the conservative response to unexpected conditions or a need for clarification [AP] (Sec 1, p. 16). Even if the matter seems simple, the person notifies the supervisor and gets help, stopping work long enough for knowledgeable people to discuss and resolve the issue [AP] (Sec 1, p. 16). Cues include persistent doubt; conditions outside those a procedure assumes or inconsistent with it; being outside key parameters or beyond the plan's scope; unexpected results; something expected not happening; uncertainty about compliance; inexperience; and someone else expressing doubt [AP] (Sec 1, p. 16). The four steps are pause, make the equipment and job site safe, notify the supervisor and get help from more knowledgeable people [AP] (Sec 1, p. 17). At-risk practices include dismissing contrary evidence, discounting less experienced people's concerns, not asking for help out of embarrassment, arguing over who is right rather than what is right, and having no clear abort criteria [AP] (Sec 1, p. 17).

### Self-Checking

Self-checking focuses the performer's attention on the right component, the intended action and its expected outcome before acting, and on verifying the result afterwards [AP] (Sec 1, p. 18). The handbook calls it particularly effective for skill-based, repetitive tasks done without much conscious thought, with attention needing to peak at the moment of greatest risk, when a component's status is changed; it also helps when recording or entering data and doing calculations [AP] (Sec 1, p. 18). Cues include manipulating equipment, physical interfaces with plant equipment, entering data, calculations, experiments, reading indicators of critical attributes, editing drawings or procedures by cut-and-paste or hand annotation, impending status changes, critical tasks identified at the briefing, and assembling components with interchangeable similar parts [AP] (Sec 1, p. 18).

The practice is STAR, Stop–Think–Act–Review [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 18–19): **Stop**, pausing before critical activities and removing distractions; **Think**, understanding what the correct action on the correct component will do, confirming conditions match the briefing and the equipment status, identifying the expected result, comparing with the controlling document, preparing a contingency, and using the FACTS questioning attitude if uncertain; **Act**, following the guidance, reading and touching the component label without losing eye contact, comparing it with the document and performing the action; **Review**, confirming the result matches the expectation, executing the contingency if it does not, and notifying the supervisor as needed. At-risk practices include not understanding a step's intent, self-checking without the guiding document, doing several manual actions in quick succession, acting despite discrepancies or while distracted, looking away from the component, not re-checking after losing contact with it, not identifying critical steps in advance, not verifying results, and working while fatigued [AP] (Sec 1, p. 19).

### Procedure Use and Adherence

Procedure adherence means understanding a procedure's intent and purpose and following its direction, performing all actions as written in the order specified; if it cannot be used safely and correctly as written, the activity stops and the procedure is revised before work continues [AP] (Sec 1, p. 20). The handbook stresses procedure quality but warns that following a procedure without question does not guarantee safety, because procedures can contain hidden flaws and do not always contain enough information; users must stay mindful of what their actions will do to equipment [AR] (Sec 1, p. 20). It is used when manipulating, monitoring or analysing equipment, whenever a procedure exists, when none exists but should (stop and get help), and when technical specifications require it [AP] (Sec 1, p. 20). The practice: confirm the working copy is the current revision; review prerequisites, limits and precautions, initial conditions and instructions, and confirm the procedure fits the equipment condition; use it at its designated level (continuous, reference or information use); follow it as written; stop, make the equipment safe and contact a supervisor if a step cannot be done as written, would cause injury or damage, would produce an incorrect or unsafe configuration, is technically wrong, gives unexpected results, conflicts with another procedure or is otherwise unsafe; and report procedure problems so important deficiencies are fixed before reuse [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 20–21). At-risk practices include no page-check, no pre-job review, not establishing initial conditions, not knowing a step's purpose or the critical steps, skipping steps of a "routine" procedure because they were unnecessary before, using a superseded revision, following a procedure known to cause harm as written, and not feeding back on accuracy and usability [AP] (Sec 1, p. 21).

### Validate Assumptions

Assumptions are a necessary part of scientific and engineering work, letting a problem be bounded while information is gathered, but knowledge workers must not let an assumption harden into fact or forget they made it [AP] (Sec 1, p. 22). The handbook places assumptions in knowledge-based work, where they reduce mental effort; lack of knowledge breeds erroneous assumptions, and the shortcut is most tempting under stress and time pressure [AR] (Sec 1, p. 22). Qualifying phrases such as *I think*, *we've always done it this way* or *we didn't have a problem last time* signal that an assumption has been made; unverifiable assumptions call for subject matter experts [AP] (Sec 1, p. 22). Cues include conceptual design or experiment phases, product review meetings, before delivery to the customer, verification of output documents, calculations, procurement, before using preliminary or unvalidated vendor data, and answering technical questions for operations [AP] (Sec 1, p. 22). The four practices are: document the assumption (its applicability, the critical attributes it affects, the reasoning, the extent of condition and worst case, and the level of certainty and conservatism); seek objective evidence (past successes, operating experience, expert opinion, reference documents, alternative techniques or simulation, technical rationale); do a field walk-down to check in-field factors; and track and close out every unverified assumption before delivering the product [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 22–23). At-risk practices include not recording or not recognising an assumption, not verifying it because the preparer seems competent, treating it as fact, not tracking closure, missing conflicting inputs across design documents, not documenting the basis of engineering judgment, not reconciling contradictory sources, and leaning too heavily on past successes [AP] (Sec 1, p. 23).

### Signature

A signature or seal on an engineering, scientific or technical product records the rigour applied to it; before releasing a product to the next step the individual signs to signify the task was done completely and accurately to all standards, procedures and codes [AP] (Sec 1, p. 24). The tool reminds the signer what the signature means and the level of scrutiny it implies; a personal signature reflects professional commitment and prompts the preparer to verify accuracy [AP] (Sec 1, p. 24). Before releasing a product the individual affirms six things [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 24–25): **Knowledge** (the expertise, qualifications and authority to sign, and an understanding of the role signed for, such as author, peer reviewer or supervisor); **Involvement** (actually prepared, reviewed or supervised it); **Independent** (the required freedom of thought from those earlier in the process); **Quality** (meets standards and codes, has appropriate safety factors and margin, satisfies design-basis requirements and is complete and correct); **Right and Proper** (believes the product is the right thing to do); and **No Doubt** (no doubts about it at this stage, and willingness to own its accuracy; otherwise stop and ask for help). At-risk practices include signing for work one did not perform or oversee, or outside one's expertise; deferring to what management wants without critical thought; defining too many approvers; not defining what the signature means; relaxing standards for expediency; relying on memory of codes; accepting everything as fact; and hurrying [AP] (Sec 1, p. 25).

### Effective Communication: Three-Way Communication and the Phonetic Alphabet

The goal of effective communication is mutual understanding, especially of technical information about operations or safety; the handbook calls it probably the most important defence against errors and events [AP] (Sec 1, p. 26). Oral communication is riskier than written, and misunderstanding is most likely when people hold different mental models of the work or use confusing terms, so verbal exchanges of operational information must be confirmed [AR] (Sec 1, p. 26).

**Three-way communication** ("repeat back") uses three exchanges [AP] (Sec 1, pp. 26–27). The sender, who is responsible for confirming the receiver understood, gets the receiver's attention (by name or position, face to face where practical) and states the message clearly and concisely. The receiver paraphrases the message back in their own words but repeats equipment designators and nomenclature word for word, asking questions if needed. The sender confirms that the read-back is correct or corrects and restates; a corrected receiver paraphrases again. It is considered for operating or altering equipment, reporting equipment condition or important parameter values, performing procedure steps, and task assignments affecting equipment, personnel, the environment or the facility [AP] (Sec 1, p. 26). At-risk practices include not identifying oneself and one's location on phone or radio, interrupting someone already in a conversation, packing too much or too little into one message, the sender not verifying understanding, the receiver not asking for clarification or acting before the exchange is complete, not writing down messages with more than two items, preoccupation, and speaking too softly or indistinctly [AP] (Sec 1, p. 27).

**The phonetic alphabet** addresses letters that sound alike (the handbook's example is D and B) in noisy or stressful conditions, over weak signals or across accents, by substituting a standard word for each letter [AP] (Sec 1, p. 28). Where two component labels differ by a single letter, that letter is spoken phonetically; the handbook's example contrasts two labels differing only in L and F [AE] (Sec 1, p. 28). It is used for alphanumeric equipment identifiers and wherever misunderstanding is likely; at-risk practices are using non-standard phonetic words and slang [AP] (Sec 1, p. 28). The standard table runs Alpha to Zulu [AP] (Sec 1, p. 28).

### Place-Keeping

Place-keeping is physically marking procedure steps as they are completed, to prevent omitting or repeating steps; the handbook explains that a user's attention shifts constantly between the procedure, controls, indicators, equipment and people, and that branching procedures with many decision points are especially exposed [AR] (Sec 1, p. 29). It matters most for status and configuration control, for reassembly after maintenance, and wherever skipping, repeating or half-completing a step could do harm; it also lets a user return to the last step after an interruption [AP] (Sec 1, p. 29). It is used for continuous-use procedures and for reference-use procedures on risk-important equipment [AP] (Sec 1, p. 29). Example techniques include blacking out non-applicable steps or highlighting applicable ones, marking critical steps conspicuously beforehand, initialling or ticking each step or action, circling a step number when in progress and slashing it when done, and annotating page completion in the margin [AP] (Sec 1, p. 29). At-risk practices include one set of initials with a line drawn through the remaining sign-off blanks, skipping familiar steps, casual use because of past success, signing off a step before it is done or several at once, ditto marks, no place-keeping on continuous-use procedures, and not checking the last step after an interruption [AP] (Sec 1, p. 30).

**Do Not Disturb sign.** When knowledge workers do risk-important or safety-critical work, especially reviews and verifications, managers must control access to them so they are not distracted; a sign at the work-space entrance, naming the task, asking that the person not be interrupted and giving the supervisor's or alternate's contact details, does this, and everyone must respect it [AP] (Sec 1, p. 31). Cues include risk-important work or technical reviews, demanding turnaround on a complex review, repetitive tasks where interruption breeds error, and whenever the preparer asks [AP] (Sec 1, p. 31). At-risk practices include not using it for risk-important work, posting it inconspicuously, others ignoring it, omitting contact details and using it without supervisor concurrence [AP] (Sec 1, p. 31).

## Part III: Tools for work teams (Sec 2)

All of Part III is paraphrased from INPO-adapted material; see the header.

### When the team tools apply

Whether to use the work-team tools depends on the task's hazards, complexity and frequency, how long the activity runs (multiple shifts or groups) and management's need for feedback; they need two or more people, supervisory involvement and management support [AP] (Sec 2, p. 33).

### Pre-Job Briefing

A pre-job briefing is a meeting of performers and supervisors before a job to go over the tasks, critical steps, hazards and precautions, and to clarify objectives, roles, responsibilities and resources; knowing clearly what one is trying to do is said to improve error recognition [AP] (Sec 2, p. 34). Its effectiveness depends on preparation: participants should arrive having done their task preview, which supports a real dialogue, lets them mentally rehearse critical steps and reinforces that there are no routine activities [AP] (Sec 2, p. 34).

The handbook grades the briefing by hazard and complexity [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 34–35). **Low-hazard, simple or repetitive** work usually needs only a mental walk-through of the task preview, with no critical steps; personal safety hazards and PPE are always reviewed, and whether to meet face to face is the supervisor's judgment. **Low-hazard, complex or infrequent** work needs a standard but thorough job-specific briefing, often from a checklist, because complexity can hide developing hazards; complexity includes many interactions with controls, simultaneous activities or procedures, heavy coordination, major status changes, unusual configurations and tool or physical constraints. **High-hazard, simple or repetitive** work, which the handbook says may describe much of the facility's work, likely has critical steps and significant potential harm; the handbook states that most events occur during so-called "routine" activities and that people wrongly equate simple or routine with no hazards, and recommends a standard checklist tailored with task-specific information. **High-hazard, complex or infrequent** evolutions likely have critical steps, high potential for harm and reduced margins, and need extra training and briefing, sometimes with mock-ups to rehearse the work. Briefings are held before work on facility equipment, once per shift for multi-shift work and after long delays [AP] (Sec 2, p. 35).

The recommended detailed agenda covers [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 35–36): purpose, scope and nature of the work; the documents to be used; assignments, roles, qualifications, personal limitations, handoffs and controlling authority; hazards and mitigations (permits, energy control, PPE, ALARA); human performance, meaning the tools to use at each critical step for nuclear, industrial, radiological and environmental safety and for production, plus special conditions, resources, partial procedures, foreign material exclusion, interactions with other work and communication obstacles; operating experience and how similar errors will be avoided; stop-work or pause criteria, contingencies, scope changes and who makes critical decisions; the degree of management oversight; and performers' questions and concerns. At-risk practices include not planning the briefing or giving people time to prepare, generalities instead of specifics, a monologue without participation, people not voicing concerns, a "cookbook" run through every checklist item regardless of relevance, being blind to how mind-sets disguise warning signs, not assigning contingency and abort responsibilities, omitting error-likely situations and defences for critical activities, noisy settings, overlong briefings, ignoring equipment history and personal experience, misjudging whether a task counts as infrequent given participants' proficiency, and irrelevant operating experience [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 36–37).

### Technical Task Pre-Job Briefing

For technical (office) tasks the briefing is fundamentally different because there is usually no hands-on work: it is a supervisor–performer discussion to assign the task, clarify roles, methods, resources and deliverables, and identify risk factors, critical parameters and compensating actions [AP] (Sec 2, p. 38). Its main purpose is to find and compensate for error-likely situations that could let a product endanger the plant or people, including discussion of how error could affect the project's critical attributes and what extra controls are needed [AP] (Sec 2, p. 38). The individual previews the task first; "reverse" briefings, where the assigned person leads, let the supervisor confirm understanding; past experience and mistakes are reviewed [AP] (Sec 2, p. 38). Cues: new assignments, before peer review or verification, at turnover, before walk-downs or inspections, after breaks of several days, and during vendor activities [AP] (Sec 2, p. 38). The practice is to assign a qualified person with regard to the task's demands and the person's skills, experience and fitness; summarise the scope, roles, critical attributes and parameters, methods, applicable codes, input data and how current it is, and key interfaces; anticipate human performance challenges using S-A-F-E-R adapted to technical work (errors per critical activity, credible and worst-case consequences if undetected, prevention and catching methods, lessons learned); and have the individual summarise in their own words the requirements, critical attributes, consequences of a defective product, abort criteria, concerns (renegotiating deadlines if needed) and their readiness to deliver a defect-free product [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 38–39). Additional at-risk practices include not using lessons learned, showing a lack of ownership, assigning someone without experience of the required processes, and not acknowledging the assigned engineer's learning curve [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 39–40).

### Checking and verification practices

The handbook groups four tools that use a second person to confirm a performer's actions or results [AP] (Sec 2, p. 41). It distinguishes **checking**, confirming a correct action so as to prevent a performer's error, from **verification**, confirming that equipment condition or document accuracy matches the governing documents. Peer-checking aims at preventing the performer's mistake; concurrent and independent verification aim at confirming the correct configuration or status of equipment or documents; peer review is a defence that detects errors and defects in another's work product (designs, calculations, procedures, work packages) before it is completed [AP] (Sec 2, p. 41).

**Peer-Checking (PC).** Two people working together at the same time and place, before and during a specific action; it supplements, never replaces, self-checking, and focuses on doing the correct act [AP] (Sec 2, p. 42). The handbook calls it the least rigorous of the checking and verification tools [AP] (Sec 2, p. 42). Both self-check, agree on the action and component, the peer watches before and during the act, stops the performer if the action diverges, and confirms when it is correct; it uses a fresh pair of eyes, is informal, can be requested by anyone and done by anyone familiar with the task and trained in the technique, though management may make it mandatory for certain actions [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 42–43). Suggested uses include critical steps, irreversible actions, comparing test data with acceptance criteria, starting or stopping major components, return to or removal from service, identifying the right part before maintenance and installing interchangeable parts [AP] (Sec 2, p. 42). At-risk practices include an inexperienced or inattentive peer, a peer who cannot see the component or is reluctant to correct a more senior performer, a peer who assumes no mistake will happen, a performer who acts before the peer is ready, each relying on the other instead of self-checking, and overuse leading to complacency [AP] (Sec 2, p. 43).

**Concurrent Verification (CV).** Two people at the same time and place separately confirm a component's condition before, during and after an action, where an incorrect condition would lead to harm; it is like PC but addresses conditions rather than actions, and the two can be combined [AP] (Sec 2, p. 44). It is usually reserved for key components where an error could cause possibly irreversible harm, with the procedure signed or initialled by both as the record [AP] (Sec 2, p. 44). The two try to keep freedom of thought, but because they work side by side true independence is impossible, so each tries to stay objective [AP] (Sec 2, p. 44). The handbook lists irreversible consequences in nuclear safety (fissile material, safety function, criticality control), industrial and radiological safety (death, injury, overexposure), environmental safety (uncontrolled discharges) and facility safety (impaired safety systems, damage, property loss) [AP] (Sec 2, p. 44). Practice: agree the action and target condition, each referring to the document separately; each self-checks; the verifier observes; each confirms the result separately, preferably hands-on, otherwise by system response or remote indication (using several indicators and, where possible, one local check); both sign [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 44–45). At-risk practices include a verifier lacking knowledge, not watching closely, or much junior and reluctant to correct; either party relying on the other or on verbal cues instead of their own check; and a performer relaxing because a verifier is present [AP] (Sec 2, p. 45).

**Independent Verification (IV).** One person, separated by time and distance from the action or document production, confirms the component's condition or the document's accuracy, used where an undetected wrong state could later cause harm [AP] (Sec 2, p. 46). The handbook says IV tends to catch more errors than PC or CV because the verifier did not change the component or produce the document and their understanding is not influenced by the performer [AR] (Sec 2, p. 46). Independence is freedom of thought: separation in time means checking after the initial alignment, separation by distance means neither can see or hear the other, so the performer does not communicate with the verifier while acting [AP] (Sec 2, p. 46). Management designates which systems, components and documents get IV and by what method; IVs may be done step by step or at the end where safe, and the procedure should say which [AP] (Sec 2, p. 46). Uses include safety-related system alignments, clearance tags, return to service after maintenance, fire protection alignment, temporary modifications, as-left instrument positions, status changes that could affect the safety basis, and verification of design and safety-basis calculations and of procedures [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 46–47). The performer self-checks, acts, confirms results, signs and notifies; the verifier self-checks, determines the as-found condition without changing it (hands-on preferred), compares with the governing document, notifies the supervisor of any disagreement, signs if it agrees and reports completion [AP] (Sec 2, p. 47). At-risk practices include walking to the component together, being co-workers on the same job, the verifier being nearby when the performer acts, relying only on process parameters (alternate flow paths can mislead), a junior verifier reluctant to question, and superficial checking in the belief that other verifiers will catch problems [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 47–48).

**Peer Review.** A reviewer reads and checks another's risk-important work product, or a decision or plan, before it is finalised; the fresh eyes may see what the preparer missed, but preparer and reviewer are equally accountable for its quality [AP] (Sec 2, p. 49). It is informal and does not replace required checklists [AP] (Sec 2, p. 49). Supporting conditions: qualified reviewers (the same or greater qualification than the preparer), a defined scope and checklists, the technical inputs, enough time, not too many reviewers (to avoid team errors), and periodic management review of work products for accountability; documenting reviews lets errors be trended and teaches others [AP] (Sec 2, p. 49). The practice is to define the review (why, who, what, when, how, and acceptance criteria), identify the product's critical attributes, then dig for facts across three readings: an overview that highlights critical attributes and failure-prone conditions; verification of data, accuracy and assumptions; and documentation of concerns and resolutions with FACTS, checking that conclusions hold and the product answers the stated problem [AP] (Sec 2, p. 50). Separate readings are said to keep the reviewer focused and reduce mental workload [AP] (Sec 2, p. 49). At-risk practices include involving the reviewer in preparing the document, using reviews to train inexperienced staff, cutting review time under schedule pressure, multitasking, interruptions, not documenting the review and lacking a questioning attitude [AP] (Sec 2, p. 50).

### Flagging

Flagging addresses events that start on the wrong one of several similar, closely spaced components, or when a person returns from a break or distraction to an adjacent wrong component [AP] (Sec 2, p. 51). After self-checking, the performer marks the correct component with an approved device (coloured dots, ribbons, tags, magnetic placards, tape) so they can find it again; flags can also mark similar components not to touch; devices must not obstruct indicators or interfere with equipment [AP] (Sec 2, p. 51). It is used near similar-looking components, for repeated manipulations, near trip-sensitive equipment and when the briefing calls for it; the steps are identify by self-checking, flag, work, remove [AP] (Sec 2, p. 51). At-risk practices include the same flags for "touch" and "don't touch", flagging without checking, flags that obscure indicators or dislodge easily (the handbook names a sticky note), leaving flags behind and conductive flag material [AP] (Sec 2, p. 51).

### Turnover

Turnover is the orderly transfer of information, tasks and responsibility between individuals or crews, giving the on-coming person time to form an accurate mental model (situation awareness) before taking over [AP] (Sec 2, p. 52). Turnovers vary with risk and work type but share the purpose of passing on what is needed to continue safely with minimal interruption; they should be thorough and accurate yet brief, and are done visually (walk-downs), verbally (with three-way communication for risk-important points) and in writing, because oral information is prone to distortion and forgetting [AR] (Sec 2, p. 52). The off-going person hands over only when confident the on-coming person is capable [AP] (Sec 2, p. 52). Cues: shift change, handoffs between people, groups or organisations, multi-shift emergent or complex work, and changes in responsibility mid-task [AP] (Sec 2, p. 52). Practice: keep a turnover log; the relieving party identifies the specific tasks, covering job and equipment status, schedule, objectives and milestones, procedures and last steps completed, problems and unusual lineups, critical steps and error-likely situations with countermeasures, resources and key contacts; discuss face to face, challenging assumptions; for operations and maintenance, independently review the log and walk down the area together; then formally transfer responsibility [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 52–53). At-risk practices include multitasking during turnover, no face-to-face explanation, leaving out critical information or the bases for decisions, not documenting, distracting settings, handing over to an unprepared person, and not scheduling time for turnover [AP] (Sec 2, p. 53).

### Post-Job Review in the field, and the technical task post-job review

Feedback on how work is initiated, planned, executed and controlled matters to management, because procedure, process, equipment, tool and supply problems and minor errors tend to be latent and to accumulate if uncorrected; a post-job review is a self-assessment after the work that solicits participants' feedback so management can remove weaknesses that could challenge event-free performance [AR] (Sec 2, p. 54). Usually a brief face-to-face meeting of performers and supervisors, it covers what went well and what could improve, and identifies lessons learned [AP] (Sec 2, p. 54). Common topics are surprises, the usability of work documents, knowledge and skill gaps, minor errors, unexpected job-site conditions and workarounds, supervisory support, tools and resources, planning and scheduling, significant lessons to record, and lingering gut feelings [AP] (Sec 2, p. 54). Managers reinforce reviews by giving timely feedback on how high-interest issues were resolved [AP] (Sec 2, p. 54). Cues: any work with complications, non-routine or important work, each high-risk phase of a risk-important project, emergent work, and routine work where improvements were identified [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 54–55). The four practices are Forum (time to talk or document feedback), Feedback (pluses and deltas, especially at critical steps, comparing what happened with what was planned), Forms (record and route them, using the corrective action programme as appropriate) and Follow Up (report resolution of high-interest issues back to performers) [AP] (Sec 2, p. 55). At-risk practices include skipping it after work on risk-important equipment, absent principal participants, no time or a rushed review, no follow-up method, follow-up not done face to face, and not recording issues for future briefings [AP] (Sec 2, p. 55).

The technical-task version states the stakes more strongly: errors that cause significant events are organisational failures, so feedback is critical, since the severity of consequences depends on organisational weaknesses; reviews give early warning of weaknesses in processes, programmes and policies that affect a technical activity's defences [AR] (Sec 2, p. 56). It emphasises flawed defences, error traps met and the consequences of problems, is held as soon as practicable after the task or each high-risk phase, and is focused rather than laborious [AP] (Sec 2, p. 56). Its five steps are Face-to-Face meeting led by the task lead, Pluses, Deltas tied to critical activities, Follow-Up, and Face-to-Face Again to report resolutions [AP] (Sec 2, p. 56). At-risk practices mirror the field version, adding responsible engineers absent [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 56–57).

### Project Planning

Project management gives structure to work with discrete start and end dates such as modifications and upgrades, keeps scope and deliverables aligned with the business plan, and minimises rework, assumptions and omissions [AP] (Sec 2, p. 58). The handbook ties it to error: failure risk comes mainly from uncertainty at every stage, part of which is the potential for human error, and the mind cannot reliably hold every element of a complex project in awareness [AR] (Sec 2, p. 58). It is used in design work, work not governed by administrative procedures and work with subcontractors, but not for core business or level-of-effort work [AP] (Sec 2, p. 58). The project work plan covers Initiate (a charter defining the problem, an accountable manager, team, purpose and scope, design authority, customers and stakeholders, and deliverables as the definition of success), Plan (organisation and accountabilities, stakeholder involvement, interfaces, field walk-down, a schedule including technical pre-job briefings and post-job reviews, error controls for critical activities, resources, workload, design inputs and reviews, lessons learned, and risk sources with error-prevention requirements covering at least verification, peer review, validation and integrated testing), Control (tracking critical activities, process adherence, meaningful indicators, conflict management, reinforcing human performance tools, change impact, review meetings, vendor monitoring, document and data control, rewards) and Close (quality and commissioning results, effectiveness, client satisfaction, lessons learned) [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 58–60). At-risk practices include poor communication, excluding stakeholders, splitting responsibility between two or more people, treating risk lightly, weak configuration control of the plan leading to scope creep, not identifying human performance controls, not publishing the plan or documenting intermediate decisions, unresolved resource conflicts, undefined scope and frequent changes of team members [AP] (Sec 2, p. 60).

### Problem Solving with PACTS

Problem solving is classed as a knowledge-based situation, with no recognisable pattern, rule or skill to apply; it chains cause and effect backward to explain why the problem exists [AP] (Sec 2, p. 61). Given that error chances in knowledge-based situations run from 1 in 2 to 1 in 10, the handbook advises pausing and involving at least one other person, including users and field staff, and using PACTS when the FACTS questioning attitude has not resolved the question [AP] (Sec 2, p. 61). The steps are **P**roblem statement (a gap between what is and what should be, agreed by stakeholders, especially those closest to the problem; large problems broken down), **A**nalysis (structured, objective, repeatable, approved methods proportionate to the problem), **C**auses (those that, if corrected, prevent recurrence and fit the facts, sensitive to supporting and refuting evidence), **T**esting (corroborate causes through testing, independent review and a questioning attitude) and **S**olution (corrective actions for each cause, weighing risk, benefit and cost) [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 61–62). At-risk practices include defining the problem in terms of causes, trying solutions before defining the problem, assuming a procedure change or training always fixes it, not taking immediate action against recurrence pending the long-term fix, relying on intuition or brainstorming for risk-important issues, naming a cause when none can be found, acting when unsure of the cause, ruling out causes without facts, letting one person dominate, leaving out stakeholders and avoiding controversy [AP] (Sec 2, p. 62).

### Decision Making

Where problem solving looks backward, decision making is described as forward-looking: anticipating the effects of alternatives and choosing the one that best meets needs within constraints; a methodical process guards against rule-based and knowledge-based errors [AP] (Sec 2, p. 63). Conservative decisions put the facility's safety needs ahead of near-term production [AP] (Sec 2, p. 63). Every decision should clarify the goal, identify options, analyse them, plan implementation and define how effectiveness will be measured [AP] (Sec 2, p. 63). Whether immediate or formal, safety requires conservatism, which the handbook promotes through staying within the safe operating envelope, using all available information and resisting the urge to discount disconfirming data, using all available expertise including front-line workers, minimising uncertainty by relying on facts and challenging assumptions, holding safety against production pressure, considering cumulative risk and preparing contingencies [AP] (Sec 2, p. 63). Leaders can assign a devil's advocate to watch for flaws, because most people focus on getting the task done rather than on what to avoid [AR] (Sec 2, p. 63). Cues include decisions with significant consequences, conceptual design of critical activities, project work plans, product reviews, troubleshooting, operability determinations, the final phases of root cause analysis and procurement of unlike replacement parts [AP] (Sec 2, p. 64). The steps are Goal (desired future state and critical attributes), Options (several alternatives), Analysis (assumptions, stakeholder effects, pros and cons, short- and long-term risks, benefits and costs, operating experience), Plan (who, what, by when; conservative on critical attributes; contingencies; abort or hold criteria; stakeholder involvement) and Review (periodic effectiveness reviews and an independent review of the proposed decision) [AP] (Sec 2, p. 64). At-risk practices include deciding before defining the goal, unstructured methods for risk-important issues, deciding without understanding the risks, and not taking immediate action against recurrence [AP] (Sec 2, p. 65).

### Project (Product) Review Meeting

Science and engineering involve judgment, uncertainty and risk, so design and experiment development need a structured team review that draws on the knowledge of affected parties and stakeholders; diverse and critical opinions are valued, and the team decides when the project is ready [AP] (Sec 2, p. 66). Meetings need a responsible chair, an agenda with times, only people with a contribution to make, clear outcomes (what, who, by when) and minutes [AP] (Sec 2, p. 66). The handbook warns that people err in meetings and team errors occur, that participants may hold inaccurate perceptions and spread serious misreadings of critical information, that open communication is key and interpersonal obstacles must be removed first, that processes for examining differing professional opinions are widely known and applied, and that a chair may designate a devil's advocate [AR] (Sec 2, p. 66). Uses include initial designs or changes to experiments or designs, changes to safety-related equipment under configuration control, complex temporary modifications and multiple points in the design process [AP] (Sec 2, p. 66). Practices: name the members, circulate the agenda and documents in advance, and expect members to attend, pre-review, submit comment sheets, voice stakeholder concerns, assign owners for commitments and avoid scope changes after the midcourse review [AP] (Sec 2, p. 67). At-risk practices include late scheduling, no agenda, stakeholders brought in late or represented inconsistently, unprepared members, absences and no follow-up on action items [AP] (Sec 2, p. 67).

### Vendor Oversight

DOE sites are run by prime contractors who may use subcontractors; limited-scope, special-project contractors are called vendors here, and the handbook says they are at high risk of involvement in significant events, with general employee training often insufficient to make up for their lack of facility experience in industrial safety, radiation protection and human performance [AP] (Sec 2, p. 68). Vendors need the same coaching as facility staff, and their work must meet facility standards even when done at their own offices [AP] (Sec 2, p. 68). The VENDOR mnemonic covers **V**alidation of vendor data and assurances with objective evidence (*trust, but verify*); **E**xpectations clearly communicated for specifications, training, qualifications and quality processes, especially industrial safety, radiological protection and error prevention; i**N**terdependency, a close cooperative working relationship; **D**ocumentation that is clear and detailed, with vendor problems logged in the corrective action or non-conformance programme; **O**versight of office and field activities through an assigned coach and a monitoring plan graded to the vendor's risk and past performance (continuous, intermittent or none); and **R**eview of deliverables against critical attributes [AP] (Sec 2, pp. 68–69). Cues range from contract preparation through award, work, equipment returns and completion, and include suspicion of improper work and use of vendor-supplied information [AP] (Sec 2, p. 68). At-risk practices include assuming the vendor is expert and will not err or shares DOE work standards, insufficiently testing vendor designs, thin in-process oversight, appearing to co-employ, and assuming the vendor grasps how changes affect its standard product [AP] (Sec 2, p. 69).

## Part IV: Management tools for finding latent weaknesses (Sec 3)

### Why managers need their own tools

Section 3's tools help managers and supervisors identify latent weaknesses, "mainly undetected deficiencies in organizational processes or values that create workplace conditions that provoke error (error precursors) or degrade the integrity of defenses (flawed defenses)" [V] (Sec 3, p. 70). "Undetected organizational deficiencies plague human performance" [V]; latent conditions are hard to find and "Once they are created they do not fade away but rather accumulate in the system" [V], so "Managers should aggressively identify and correct vulnerabilities with defenses at the earliest opportunity" [V] (Sec 3, p. 70). The section lists benchmarking, observations, self-assessments, performance indicators, independent oversight, work product review, investigating events triggered by human error, operating experience, change management, reporting errors and near misses, and employee surveys [AP] (Sec 3, p. 70).

### Benchmarking

Benchmarking compares one's own performance in an area with organisations that do better and learns what they do; it is "the process of measuring products, services, and practices against the toughest competitors or those companies recognized as industry leaders" [V] (Sec 3, p. 71). Managers first evaluate their own performance to agree the gaps to close, then find exemplary organisations willing to share, usually through extensive communication and a site visit; some organisations treat it as continuous [AP] (Sec 3, p. 71). "Benchmarking is a powerful management tool because it overcomes “Paradigm Blindness.”" [V], the mind-set that the current way is best because it is the way things have always been done, or that nothing can be learned from others who do not understand one's situation [AP] (Sec 3, p. 71). It cracks resistance to change by showing that other methods work because others use them [AP] (Sec 3, p. 71). Cues: an inefficient, ineffective, costly or risky process; rising errors and near misses in an area; a wide gap from ideal performance; a recognised need for dramatic improvement [AP] (Sec 3, p. 71). The six steps run from identifying the problem area with both quantitative and qualitative data, through finding comparable organisations, selecting a "best in class" partner, setting protocols and exchanging information, visiting, to evaluating and implementing with local conditions in mind and selling the ideas locally [AP] (Sec 3, p. 72). At-risk practices include not pinpointing the process to improve, cutting short data collection, choosing partners that are merely different rather than best in class, ignoring management-system differences that block adaptation, unwillingness to share, and failing to follow through after visits, "falling into the category of “industrial tourism”" [V] (Sec 3, p. 72).

### Observations

Field observation of individual performance shows how well the organisation supports work at the job site; it reviews the quality of preparation, practices and performance, and "The purpose is not to criticize or to judge people" [V]: the main objective is to find improvements to the organisation of work while watching people work [AP] (Sec 3, p. 73). "The scope of observations should include the whole job, not just performer behavior" [V]: observers also watch the job-site context, hazards and controls, and record results for trending [AP] (Sec 3, p. 73). "Behavior observations can flush out organizational weaknesses that may not be obvious by any other means" [V], and "When managers and supervisors spend time in the field with individuals doing work, performance improves—error rates tend to decrease" [V] (Sec 3, p. 73). The practice: plan around specific activities and critical steps; know the task's likely errors and performers' weaknesses; remove obstacles; check tools, parts and skills; reinforce and coach; correct at-risk practices on the spot; ask questions that surface error precursors and latent weaknesses (whether the procedures were accurate, resources and training sufficient, planning and scheduling set up to reduce error, processes supportive, supervision helpful, and whether the supervisor knows of performance traps that could cause error next time); record findings for trending; and follow up [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 73–74). At-risk practices include not planning, unwillingness to be critical and intrusive, not asking hard questions, not stopping at-risk behaviour, "Focusing totally on the individual’s behaviors, and ignoring job-site conditions and organizational processes and values that support individual performance" [V], giving no feedback, not recording or trending, and not correcting the weaknesses observed [AP] (Sec 3, p. 74).

### Self-Assessments

Self-assessment compares present practices and results with desired ones; "Because no one knows better how things are done in the facility than those working in the performing organizations, self-assessments can be the most effective means of identifying latent weaknesses in the organization and in the facility" [V] (Sec 3, p. 75). Self-assessments are required by DOE Order 226.1A; this tool does not replace that programme but helps managers use its information to evaluate processes and values and find conditions that weaken defences or set people up for failure [AP] (Sec 3, p. 75). Cues: a scheduled plan, waning human performance, misalignment with goals, and checking compliance [AP] (Sec 3, p. 75). The nine steps: choose the processes to assess (a multi-year list if needed, updated annually); define performance objectives including human performance principles; choose measures with regard to risk, prior results, lessons learned and resources; schedule, concentrating on problem areas; assign responsibilities; conduct the assessment without disrupting work, the objective being "to see workplace activities and conditions as is customary and not contrived for the benefit of the assessment" [V]; document results including what is going well; correct weaknesses; and re-assess after significant corrective actions to confirm they worked without serious unintended consequences [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 75–76). At-risk practices include picking easy areas, unrealistic objectives, unreliable measures, gaps in coverage, unprepared assessors, not reporting back, not taking corrective action and "Conducting the self-assessment on a deliberately staged work process" [V] (Sec 3, p. 76).

### Performance Indicators

Indicators measure an organisation's critical success factors, telling people whether planned activities are happening as intended and warning of developing problems [AP] (Sec 3, p. 77). **Lagging** indicators measure results and outcomes, showing where one is but not predicting what comes next; **leading** indicators measure system conditions and organisational "health" and forecast future performance [AP] (Sec 3, p. 77). Selecting them is hard: "Frequently, things are counted because they can be, but provide little insight as to how the organization is functioning now and no clue to future performance" [V] (Sec 3, p. 77). Examples of lagging indicators include lost-time injuries per 200,000 hours worked, collective radiation exposure, contamination events, rework, repeat maintenance within 18 months, recurring corrective actions and recurring causal factors; leading examples include time to implement corrective actions, overtime and absenteeism, the self-reporting ratio (problems found by workers against all problems found), backlogs, culture surveys, numbers of field observations, suggestions per person per month and employee concerns submitted [AP] (Sec 3, p. 77). Trend analysis is a further challenge: with sparse data "a single event could appear to be a trend" [V], rolling averages do not help, and statistical analysis is needed to avoid knee-jerk responses; "beyond selecting the “right” metrics, they must be properly analyzed to achieve their real value" [V] (Sec 3, pp. 77–78).

Selection steps: clarify the result statement precisely (and what kind of change is meant: a situation, condition, knowledge, attitude or behaviour); brainstorm candidates inclusively, considering what a measurement signals and its unintended consequences; rate each against seven criteria, namely direct, objective, adequate, quantitative where possible, disaggregated where appropriate, practical and reliable, using a simple matrix and a 1–5 scale; pick the best set, remembering that "Leading indicators are more valuable than lagging indicators, but normally more difficult to select and use" [V] and limiting each objective to two or three indicators; then set the analysis method, with an owner, targets, limits, trending method, statistical expertise and back-testing on past data [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 78–79). At-risk practices include measuring what is easy, lacking management agreement on the indicators, collecting data and doing nothing with it, and having too many indicators of poor usefulness [AP] (Sec 3, p. 79).

### Independent Oversight

Reviews by outside bodies (independent QA, DOE oversight groups, consultants, regulators, the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board) can reveal blind spots and latent conditions that would otherwise stay hidden, and practices that fall short of best practice [AP] (Sec 3, p. 80). DOE P 226.1A sets the Department-wide oversight policy, DOE O 226.1A implements it, and DOE O 470.2B describes the formal independent oversight programme under the Office of Independent Oversight (HS-60) [BT] (Sec 3, p. 80). "An external independent assessment is essentially a reverse benchmarking exercise" [V]: instead of travelling to learn from best-in-class organisations, an outside team comes to compare the operation with industry standards [AP] (Sec 3, p. 80). Most assessments are not invited, so managers tend to assume something must be wrong; committed managers resent outsiders, and "Telling a manager his/her operation is below par and requires correcting has the same affect as telling a young mother her baby is ugly—they both become defensive" [V] (Sec 3, p. 80). Yet outsiders "may spot troubled areas and process weaknesses far more readily than individuals living within the system" [V], and managers gain most when they stay dispassionate and remember that the assessment evaluates processes, practices and behaviours, not individuals [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 80–81). Practice: designate points of contact, hold daily status briefings, attend in-process and close-out debriefs, review the draft report for accuracy, share the reports internally, write a corrective action plan with owners, causal analysis for systemic weaknesses, preventive actions, dates, tracking and closure verification, implement it, and follow up with management self-assessments to make sure the changes are ingrained [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 81–82). At-risk practices include defensiveness, excluding staff (diluting ownership), and a cursory analysis that misses systemic weaknesses "so the mindset that the “system is fine” prevails and nothing really changes" [V], and not confirming that corrective actions are implemented [AP] (Sec 3, p. 82).

### Work Product Review

Supervisors periodically review knowledge workers' products face to face, identifying strengths to share and areas to improve, and use the results to coach and reinforce expectations; risk-important products get routine reviews, and checklists and grades help track improvement [AP] (Sec 3, p. 83). The practice: sample products; use a checklist of attributes (examples include the problem statement, project work plan, outcomes affecting critical attributes, methods, operating experience, risks and user-centred design, code compliance, implementation and testing, input data, assumptions, software, procedure accuracy and usability, approvals, procedural obstacles, surprises and the human performance tools used); review with a cross-functional team for pluses, deltas and minuses; grade and trend [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 83–84). The grades are "Excellent: no defects identified or errors found with the delivered product" [V]; "Satisfactory: errors with little or no impact on product quality or its conclusions" [V]; "Unsatisfactory: several errors found, or minor rework required" [V]; and "Unacceptable: errors that require significant rework or changes to product conclusions, invalidating the integrity of the product" [V] (Sec 3, p. 84). Follow-up includes recognition or condition reports and face-to-face feedback, with specific feedback on excellent, unsatisfactory and unacceptable grades [AP] (Sec 3, p. 84). At-risk practices include cursory reviews done only to meet a quota, no cross-functional view, not holding subordinate managers accountable for doing reviews, and reviewing too late to feed back into repetitive work [AP] (Sec 3, p. 84).

### Investigating Events Triggered by Human Error

Paraphrased in full; see the header. The handbook contrasts a traditional view, in which events are caused by shortfalls in people's competence, attention or attitude (labelled loss of situation awareness, violation or poor management), with a newer view in which human error is a symptom of deeper trouble in the system rather than its cause, latent organisational conditions set up error and determine how severe its consequences are, and error is connected to people's tools, tasks and environment [AR] (Sec 3, p. 85). On that view error is where an investigation starts, not where it ends, and the aim is to prevent recurrence rather than to find someone to punish [AR] (Sec 3, p. 85).

The handbook warns that investigations are distorted by hindsight, the investigator's knowledge of facts the people involved did not or could not know; traditional investigators interview participants only after mastering the requirements and the event's details, which disposes them to look for evidence of individual shortcomings, and explaining what people should have done says nothing about why they did what they did [AR] (Sec 3, p. 85). It recommends asking why the actions seemed appropriate at the time, reconstructing the situation that shaped people's decisions (their environment, not their minds), and interviewing participants before acquiring detailed knowledge of the event, so that context, which it calls the key to a successful investigation, is understood without bias [AR] (Sec 3, p. 85). The tool is for use when preventing recurrence matters more than punishment, and for finding the latent conditions that created error-likely situations or weakened defences [AP] (Sec 3, p. 85).

The steps run as follows [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 86–88). Debrief each participant: let them tell the story, tell it back to check understanding, identify the critical junctures where decisions or actions were needed, and at each juncture probe what cues they noticed, what knowledge and past experience they drew on, what they expected and what options they thought they had, and how other operations or organisational influences shaped their interpretation. A table of probe questions groups them under cues, interpretation, likely errors, previous experience and knowledge (including training and applicable rules), goals and goal conflicts, taking action (time pressure, sense of influence, whether options were weighed) and outcome (whether it matched expectations). Then review each person's job-site conditions and records; assemble the data into a sequence of events; lay it out in context-specific language organised by time and space; divide it into episodes that make sense in the domain (the handbook's example is the taxi-out before take-off) [AE]; establish what data was available to people in each episode, how process parameters were changing and how they were displayed, and which of them actually influenced behaviour; and reconstruct each person's knowledge, goals and focus of attention, explaining why their assessments or actions made sense to them, on the principle that people act reasonably given their knowledge, objectives, viewpoint and limited resources, which the handbook calls the most laborious step [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 86–88). Using Volume 1's Anatomy of an Event model, the investigator then identifies the tasks tied to the initiating action, the defences that failed to prevent, catch or mitigate the individual's error and those that failed to protect the facility, the job-site conditions and error precursors that provoked errors or encouraged violations, and, for each, the organisational process or cultural contributors [AP] (Sec 3, p. 88).

At-risk practices include learning too much about the event before debriefing, not debriefing everyone, not establishing people's frame of mind, poor reconstruction of the sequence, assuming the system is sound and free of latent weaknesses, ignoring the front-end error investigation in the back-end analysis of defences and organisational contributors, and concluding that people did not act reasonably without identifying why [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 88–89).

### Operating Experience

The case for an operating experience (OE) programme rests on the claim that "serious accidents are almost always preceded by less serious “precursor events.”" [V] (Sec 3, p. 90). A precursor event shares some features of a serious accident but falls short of significant consequence; component and system failures happen in all major facilities, usually with little safety consequence but often with human and organisational contributions, and if their fundamental causes are not corrected they recur and, combined with other failures or errors, lead to more serious events [AR] (Sec 3, p. 90). "Therefore, an effective Operating Experience (OE) program is a key factor in maintaining the strength of the defense-in-depth concept" [V] (Sec 3, p. 90). Its rationale is to learn from one's own and others' successes, failures and near misses; find processes to improve by industry practice; spot local conditions like those that caused problems elsewhere; identify precursors; detect emerging trends; and recommend preventive steps [AP] (Sec 3, p. 90). OE is defined broadly as "all events, conditions, observations, and new information that could affect how work is conducted" [V], including operating events, failures and errors whether or not they caused an accident, adverse safety conditions, organisational and human-factor issues such as degraded safety culture or high error rates, external challenges such as severe weather or security threats, and successes [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 90–91). Uses include sharing brief cases with points to consider, giving lessons just in time, drawing on job work history, combating "the natural human tendency to think “It can’t happen here”" [V], and spreading good practices [AP] (Sec 3, p. 91). Under DOE Order 210.2 and a contractor OE coordinator, the steps are collect, screen for safety significance, analyse local applicability, distribute, develop and track corrective actions (watching for organisational issues such as degraded safety culture and latent weaknesses), develop lessons from successes and feed them into training, planning, design and operations, follow up, and measure programme effectiveness [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 91–92). At-risk practices include forgetting lessons over time, doing nothing with others' experience, looking only at local OE, not tracking effectiveness and not using OE in training or outside operations [AP] (Sec 3, p. 92).

### Change Management

Change management is defined as "a methodical planning process to establish the direction of change, align people and resources, and implement the selected modification throughout an organization, large or small" [V] (Sec 3, p. 93). The handbook argues that it is usually kept for large-scale change, yet "most daily management activity involves some degree of change, such as changes in crew composition, maintenance schedule, policies, procedures, and equipment" [V], and that structured change reduces managers' own error: "Without a structured approach to planning and implementing change, the error potential for managers and the support staff is unacceptably greater" [V] (Sec 3, p. 93). It offers one change process among many, chosen because it relates to human performance improvement [AP] (Sec 3, p. 93), in eleven steps: create a vision; consult the people affected and establish urgency; consider the new values, attitudes and beliefs needed; develop a vision-oriented plan using human performance principles, front-line input and an accurate self-assessment; identify a management champion with authority over resources; consider an advisory steering committee; communicate repeatedly through multiple forums; empower people by educating them and removing process barriers; implement and reinforce desired behaviour; generate and reward short-term successes; and persevere, consolidating gains in processes and leadership attention [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 93–94). At-risk practices include no clear vision, not involving or informing those affected, not establishing urgency or shared understanding, ignoring the values and beliefs needed, assuming people already understand the change, and impatience [AP] (Sec 3, p. 94).

### Reporting Errors and Near Misses

DOE contractors gather workers' feedback through employee concerns programmes, hotlines, briefings, walk-downs, post-job reviews, suggestion forms, safety meetings and committees, and workers are generally conscientious about reporting physical hazards, facility deficiencies, equipment issues, security problems and work-process problems [AP] (Sec 3, p. 95). Organisations that embrace human performance principles strongly encourage reporting of errors and near misses, using them to find organisational problems and to help people learn, and the handbook calls the lessons from patterns of failure free [AP] (Sec 3, p. 95). "However, most organizations do not do a good job of acquiring feedback on human errors" [V]; the tool sets out the prerequisites for an error reporting system, and "It must be recognized that a change in culture may be required within many organizations before an error reporting system can be undertaken" [V] (Sec 3, p. 95). Uses include learning the nature and extent of active errors, changing error-provoking practices, strengthening training, and when management is ready to look beyond the tip of the iceberg [AP] (Sec 3, p. 96).

The prerequisites are paraphrased; see the header. The first, which the handbook calls required, is a just culture: management balances its response to unintentional errors against wilful violations, with no tolerance for reckless conduct and broad confidence that most unintended unsafe acts, being honest errors, will go unpunished [AP] (Sec 3, p. 96). That means ending the practice of naming, blaming, shaming and retraining people for honest errors, an error being an unintended departure from expected behaviour; the handbook criticises judging people by the consequence rather than the intent of their actions, so that the same act is disciplined when it leads to an event and ignored when it does not, and an inadvertent error is treated like an intentional violation [AR] (Sec 3, p. 96).
