The organisation adopts a method for judging culpability in serious incidents, the handbook naming the Foresight Test (would peers recognise the behaviour as likely to raise the chance of a safety-critical error), a Culpability Test (impairment, horseplay, unwarranted shortcuts or knowingly substandard tools or parts point to greater culpability), the Substitution Test (would a peer with similar skills and training, in the same circumstances as perceived at the time, have acted differently; if not, blame is likely inappropriate) and the Culpability Decision Tree, referring to Volume 1, Chapter 4, for detail [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 96–97). Reckless violators are held accountable so that people see the balance is right; once people know honest mistakes and organisationally induced errors will not be punished, the climate is ready for reporting [AP] (Sec 3, p. 97).

The handbook then pairs four common barriers with solutions [AP] (Sec 3, p. 97): reluctance to confess blunders (de-identification through anonymity or confidentiality, each with trade-offs for follow-up and willingness to report); fear that a report will count against the reporter (management indemnity for self-reporting, and separating the group that collects reports from any that can discipline); scepticism that management will act (rapid, useful, accessible feedback, without which reporting dries up); and the time and effort involved (easy access and free-form input). The rollout, carried out with a human performance improvement committee or equivalent, is to explain the system and how its information will be used, appoint an event report coordinator to track, trend and feed back, design an easy report form with designators that help reveal latent weaknesses, make it available at the desktop, give example reports, encourage and reinforce reporting, track and trend errors to find high-risk areas, and use the data in training and lessons learned [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 97–98). At-risk practices include "Launching a reporting system without first establishing a Just Culture" [V], not addressing the reporting barriers, collecting data and doing nothing with it, using reports in unintended ways, not reinforcing reporting and not giving timely feedback [AP] (Sec 3, p. 98).

### Culpability Decision Tree

Paraphrased; see the header. A one-page logic diagram takes a manager through a sequence of questions about an unsafe act: whether the actions were intended, whether the consequences were intended, whether expectations were knowingly violated, whether expectations were available, intelligible and correct, whether the act passes the substitution test, whether there were deficiencies in training, assignment or experience, whether the person has a history of performance problems, and whether the problem was self-reported [AP] (Sec 3, p. 99). Its outcomes range along a spectrum from increasing individual culpability (intentional act to cause harm, possible reckless violation, possible negligent error) to increasing organisational culpability (organisation-induced violation, organisation-induced error, and organisation-induced error with remediation), with a prompt to evaluate the relevant organisational processes and management and supervisory practices [AP] (Sec 3, p. 99). The Reporting section adds that the tree is used with the organisation's accountability policy to gauge individual culpability (intentional harm, reckless violation, negligent error) against organisational culpability (induced violation, induced error) [AP] (Sec 3, p. 97). The diagram's arrows do not survive conversion, so this reference does not reconstruct which answer leads to which box.

### Employee surveys

DOE's introduction says surveys can be used once as a gap analysis or periodically to monitor employee values and beliefs; "Survey results help managers determine where their time and effort can be applied most effectively to address concerns, misunderstandings, and inappropriate values" [V], and surveys have proved useful in revealing human performance awareness issues (Sec 3, p. 101). Uses include assessing employees' beliefs about safety culture, starting an HPI initiative, trending perceptions, responding to rising human performance factors in mishaps, and finding latent weaknesses [AP] (Sec 3, p. 101). Practice: follow site rules on human-subject surveys to protect privacy; validate and adapt the questions; plan administration; tell people the purpose and how results will be used; administer (electronically if possible); analyse and get management concurrence; build an action plan; and report results and the plan back to the workforce [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 101–102). At-risk practices include unvalidated questions, uncontrolled administration, not informing the workforce, not keeping management informed, doing nothing with the data and not feeding results back to participants [AP] (Sec 3, p. 102).

The three instruments are paraphrased; see the header.

- **Organizational Safety Climate Assessment Survey (OSCAS)** (pp. 103–111): adapted from a Naval Postgraduate School command safety climate survey, it gauges employees' attitudes and perceptions of operational practices from a safety perspective, with the primary goal of finding and correcting latent organisational conditions that could increase the potential for mishaps [BT] (Sec 3, p. 103). Its agree–disagree items (five-point scale plus N/A or don't know) cover procedure review, hazard reporting, training and qualification, leadership involvement in safety, high-risk task management, error management and latent weaknesses, freedom to report without repercussion, peer influence on violations, enforcement, quality standards, corner-cutting, experience levels, risk assessment and risk management, resources and overtime, briefings, over-commitment, trust in supervisors, the standing of the safety officer and department, communication up and down and across organisations, morale, and backups for human error during high-risk operations; it closes with two open questions on the most hazardous activity and the most significant improvement [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 104–111).
- **Human Performance Gap Analysis Tool** (pp. 112–120): adapted from INPO's *Human Performance Fundamentals Course Reference*, for a site leadership team to rate attributes drawn from top-performing organisations [BT] (Sec 3, p. 112). Each member rates independently, from their own understanding rather than performance reports, on a four-level scale from strength through satisfactory and worrisome to problem; results are summarised and sorted by the number of problem ratings, can be anonymous or by department, and feed facilitated discussions, self-assessment focus and outside assistance visits [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 112–113). Seven attribute groups cover leadership commitment and clear expectations; processes and values built on defence-in-depth that allows for human fallibility; training, coaching and reward practices; individual intolerance of error-likely situations and accountability; continuous improvement and self-identification of problems; management assessment and trending; and a culture of respect, fairness and honesty [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 114–120).
- **Job-Site Conditions Self-Assessment Questionnaire** (pp. 122–127): adapted from the same INPO publication, for supervisors and managers doing human-performance self-assessments [BT] (Sec 3, p. 122). Its yes/no questions, all phrased so that "yes" means no problem, are split into task-related issues controlled by the organisation and individual-related issues, and into three parts: direction to act (directives, knowledge or cues that prompt action), opportunity to act (conditions that make the action achievable) and willingness to act (the match between individual motives and job incentives), which the handbook calls the stimulus–response components of behaviour [AP] (Sec 3, p. 122). Isolated "no" answers flag potential weaknesses for investigation and clustered ones call for immediate management attention; completing it requires document review, observation and interviews [AP] (Sec 3, p. 122). The introduction calls self-assessment the most powerful tool for locating latent weaknesses and this questionnaire a very strong supporting tool [AP] (Sec 3, p. 122). The questions range over procedures and job aids, schedule time, role models, clear goals and standards, the quality of feedback, error traps and precursors, qualification and fitness, tools, materials, access and the human–machine interface, forcing functions, teamwork and ambient conditions, pay, rewards and their scheduling, reinforcement of safe and unsafe behaviour, hidden incentives to perform poorly, work-group norms and allegiance, autonomy, the fairness of the accountability policy, and whether people feel safe in their jobs even if they err occasionally [AP] (Sec 3, pp. 123–127).

## Part V: Definitions

The closing definitions give the volume's working vocabulary [AP] (Definitions, pp. 128–130). Among them: **active error**, "An error that changes equipment, system, or plant state, triggering immediate, undesired consequences" [V] (Definitions, p. 128); **at-risk practice**, "A behavior, belief, assumption, or condition that tends to diminish the effectiveness of a human performance tool or that increases the chance of error during an action" [V] (Definitions, p. 128); **checking**, "The act of confirming the actions of a performer are correct, without error" [V], against **verification**, "The act of confirming that the condition of a component, or other product of human performance, conforms to the condition required by a guiding document" [V] (Definitions, pp. 128, 130); **critical attributes**, risk-related aspects of engineering activities that could directly affect safety margins, configuration, operability, single-point vulnerabilities, control of human error at critical steps, the environment and other listed concerns [AP] (Definitions, p. 128); **critical step**, "A procedural step or series of steps or an action that, if performed improperly, will cause irreversible harm to plant equipment or people, or that will significantly affect facility operation" [V] (Definitions, p. 129); **defect**, "An undesired result of an error committed earlier in the engineering process, which becomes embedded in either the physical plant or design bases documentation" [V] (Definitions, p. 129); **error precursors**, task-related conditions that provoke error, "otherwise referred to as “risk factors.”" [V], with time pressure, first-time activity, lack of knowledge or experience and interruptions as examples [AP] (Definitions, p. 129); **independent**, freedom of thought between performer and verifier created by separation in distance and time [AP] (Definitions, p. 129); **latent condition**, undetected circumstances "such as equipment flaws, a willingness to sacrifice safety margin for immediate production goals, and various process, program, and procedure deficiencies that remain hidden until revealed by periodic testing, self-assessment processes, operating experience, or an event" [V] (Definitions, p. 130); **latent error**, an act or decision that unknowingly embeds an undesired condition in processes, culture, configuration or design bases, or reduces reliability, and stays hidden until later operations reveal it [AP] (Definitions, p. 130); **team error**, "A breakdown of one or more members of a work group that allows other individual members of the same group to err because of either a mistaken perception of another's abilities or the lack of accountability within the individual's group" [V] (Definitions, p. 130); and **uneasiness**, "An attitude of wariness or apprehension regarding the capacity of individuals to err" [V] (Definitions, p. 130). The three performance modes are defined too: skill-based as highly practised actions in familiar situations from memory, rule-based as selecting stored if–then rules from recognising the situation, and knowledge-based as a response to a totally unfamiliar situation relying on understanding of the system and fundamentals [AP] (Definitions, pp. 129–130).

## Part VI: How the tools map to error types (as the source states it)

The handbook does not tabulate tools against error types; the statements below are those it makes in the tool texts, gathered here. Each is paraphrased from INPO-adapted material except the Section 3 and Definitions entries.

- **Skill-based (slips and lapses at the point of action).** Situational-awareness tools are said to be particularly helpful in skill-mode work (Sec 1, p. 5); self-checking is particularly effective for skill-based, repetitive tasks done with little conscious thought, with attention peaking when a component's status changes (Sec 1, p. 18). Place-keeping targets omitted or repeated steps as attention shifts (Sec 1, p. 29); flagging targets returning to a wrong but similar component after a distraction (Sec 2, p. 51); the Do Not Disturb sign targets interruptions to repetitive or critical work (Sec 1, p. 31); three-way communication and the phonetic alphabet target misheard or misunderstood messages (Sec 1, pp. 26–28) [AP].
- **Rule-based.** Procedure Use and Adherence and Validate Assumptions are singled out as having particular value for rule-based work (Sec 1, p. 5); cookbooking and over-reliance on rules of thumb are said to lead eventually to rule-based errors, which the planning-stage questioning attitude helps prevent (Sec 1, p. 13); a methodical decision-making process guards against rule-based and knowledge-based errors (Sec 2, p. 63) [AP].
- **Knowledge-based.** Pause When Unsure is framed around the knowledge-based mode, with a 10–50 percent error chance (Sec 1, p. 16); assumptions arise in knowledge-based work (Sec 1, p. 22); problem solving with PACTS is itself a knowledge-based situation with error chances of 1:2 to 1:10, calling for at least one more person (Sec 2, p. 61); decision making guards against knowledge-based errors (Sec 2, p. 63) [AP].
- **Actions versus conditions.** Peer-checking prevents a wrong action by the performer; concurrent and independent verification confirm the resulting condition of equipment or documents, independent verification tending to catch errors more often than the other two; peer review detects errors and defects in work products (Sec 2, pp. 41–46) [AP].
- **Active versus latent.** Sections 1 and 2 aim at active errors at the job site; Section 3's tools aim at latent organisational weaknesses that provoke error or degrade defences (Introduction, p. 1; Sec 3, p. 70) [AP]. The Definitions distinguish an active error, which immediately changes plant state, from a latent error and a defect, which embed undesired conditions that stay hidden until revealed later (Definitions, pp. 128–130) [AP].

## Connections the author makes in the text

- **Institute of Nuclear Power Operations (INPO).** Named in the Foreword as the source of the primary references for the individual and work-team tools (*Human Performance Tools for Workers*, April 2006; *A Tool Kit of Proactive Industry Practices to Prevent Errors and Events*, revised March 2005), whose tools reflect years of INPO members' experience; as one source of the management tools; as the source of the Gap Analysis Tool and Job-Site Conditions Questionnaire (*Human Performance Fundamentals Course Reference*, INPO 2006-03); and as the reference for configuration control (AP-929); approving [BT] (Foreword, p. i; Sec 3, pp. 112, 122; Definitions, p. 128).
- **Naval Postgraduate School.** Source of the *Command Safety Climate Assessment Survey* from which OSCAS is adapted; neutral [BT] (Sec 3, p. 103).
- **DOE Human Performance Improvement Handbook, Volume 1.** The companion volume whose tools this one describes, cited for the culpability methods (Vol. 1, Ch 4) and drawn on for the Anatomy of an Event model; approving [BT] (Foreword, p. ii; Sec 3, pp. 88, 96).
- **NNSA, *Activity Level Work Planning and Control Processes* (2006).** Recommended for work planning and control at the activity level; approving [BT] (Introduction, p. 1; Sec 1, p. 13).
- **DOE Guide to Good Practices series and Conduct of Operations; Integrated Safety Management; Quality Assurance.** The requirements and guidance the tools enhance; approving [BT] (Foreword, pp. i–ii).
- **DOE oversight directives** (DOE P 226.1A, DOE O 226.1A, DOE O 470.2B, DOE Order 210.2) and the Defense Nuclear Facilities Safety Board. Cited for self-assessment, independent oversight and the corporate OE programme; neutral [BT] (Sec 3, pp. 75, 80, 91).

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Mindless tool use.* "Safety is not obtained by mindlessly applying human performance tools" (Introduction, p. 1); "cookbooking" procedures as mindless compliance that leads to rule-based errors (Sec 1, p. 13).
- *Treating the handbook as a requirements list.* "This handbook is not a requirements document" (Foreword, p. ii); organisations should not change effective tools (Foreword, p. ii).
- *"Routine" as "no risk".* Repeatedly named as an at-risk belief; most events occur during so-called routine activities (Sec 1, pp. 9, 11; Sec 2, pp. 34–35).
- *Following procedures blindly.* Procedures can carry hidden flaws; compliance without question does not guarantee safety (Sec 1, p. 20).
- *The traditional view of investigation.* Events blamed on individual competence, attention or attitude, investigated with hindsight to find people to punish (Sec 3, p. 85).
- *Punishing honest errors and judging by consequence.* Naming, blaming, shaming and retraining for honest errors, and disciplining the same act only when it has a consequence (Sec 3, p. 96).
- *"Paradigm blindness" and "industrial tourism".* The belief that the current way is best, and benchmarking visits with no follow-through (Sec 3, pp. 71–72).
- *Counting what is easy to count.* Indicators chosen because they can be measured (Sec 3, pp. 77, 79).
- *Observation as judging people.* "The purpose is not to criticize or to judge people" (Sec 3, p. 73).
- *Defensiveness toward independent oversight.* Becoming defensive and missing the chance to learn (Sec 3, pp. 80, 82).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

**Conversion.** PDF (137 pages, 2.2 MB, SHA-256 `ebe1e008…af53d4cc`) converted with `markitdown 0.1.8` (deterministic; no model-mediated extraction), the same converter family as Volume 1 (`markitdown 0.1.5`). Post-conversion check: 36,491 words against 33,023 words from `pdftotext` on the same PDF, about 270 words per page; the cover, the Foreword, every page footer from i to iv and 1 to 130, the Definitions and the concluding material (review activity, preparing activity, area-office list) are present; no truncation marker. The printed page numbers survive as standalone footer lines and are the citation anchors; the running header "DOE-HDBK-1028-2009 / Human Performance Tools" repeats on every page.

**Conversion damage, and how it was handled.** Body prose and bullet lists converted cleanly, though bullets render as a private-use glyph and some two-column bullet lists interleave (the Section 1 tool list, p. 5). The "When to Use HPI Tools" matrix (pp. 3–4) breaks into fragments with row labels separated from their cells, so its cell assignments are not reported. The investigation probe-question table (pp. 86–87) loses its column structure, the Anatomy of an Event figure (p. 88) and the Culpability Decision Tree (p. 99) survive only as scattered or interleaved fragments without arrows, and the survey instruments' two-column layouts (pp. 104–127) interleave items and answer scales. None of these is quoted; all are third-party or INPO-adapted material and are paraphrased from the parts whose reading order is clear. The FACTS steps (p. 14) lose their numbering after step 1: "Confirm" and "Test" appear as unnumbered paragraph heads and "Ask open-ended questions" and "Stop when unsure" as bullets.

**Third-party material.** See the header line. The decision to paraphrase all of Sections 1 and 2 rests on the Foreword's statement that their tools' primary references come from two INPO guides; it is narrower than a blanket rule only in that the Foreword, Introduction, Section 3 prose and Definitions remain quotable. Every `[V]` quotation in this reference is from the Foreword, the Introduction, the non-excepted Section 3 prose or the Definitions.

**Source inconsistencies, recorded as found.** The individual stop tool is "Pause When Unsure" in its heading and the table of contents but "Stop When Unsure" in the matrix and "Stop when unsure" in the Section 1 tool list (pp. iii, 3, 5, 16). The work-team list and table of contents say "Project Review Meeting" while the tool text speaks of "Product Review Meetings" (pp. iv, 33, 66). The Section 1 list names "Questioning attitude – in the office or lab" for the tool headed "Work Planning and Preparation" (pp. 5, 13). Procedure Use and Adherence has two steps numbered 5 (pp. 20–21). Performance Indicators numbers its selection steps 1, 2, 3, 10, 11 (pp. 78–79). The Employee Surveys introduction calls the first instrument the "Organizational Safety Climate Assessment Questionnaire" and its own page calls it a "Survey" (pp. 101, 103); its items run to 59 with 48 used twice and a stray "12." in item 47 (pp. 109–110). The definition of error reads "unintentionally depart from an unexpected behavior" (Definitions, p. 129). The at-risk footnote reads "could but workers in harms way" (Introduction, p. 2). The Foreword's formula appears as "R + M → ØE" with subscripts e and c set on the next line (p. i), where Volume 1 writes "Re + Mc → ØE". The Gap Analysis and Job-Site Conditions sources give the INPO publication number as "2006-03" (pp. 112, 122). The Pre-Job Briefing tool refers to the task preview as "individual tool #1" (p. 34), consistent with its place first in Section 1.

**Citation style.** `(Sec N, p. M)` using the handbook's printed page numbers, chosen because the converted text preserves them as footers on every page; the handbook has sections, not chapters.
